notes: Community pack, roadmap Phase 1 candidate. 5 tracks x 10 themes x 5 grade bands = 250 blocks. Expanded by tools/generate_pack.py.

tracks.name: Law: the system you already live in

themes.description: Constitutions, statutes, regulations, case law and bylaws — the layers of law and which one governs the thing in front of you.
themes.transfer_check: For one everyday rule that binds you, identify which layer of law it comes from and find its actual text.

bands.K–2: Name a classroom rule and who made it, with a teacher's help.
bands.3–5: Explain the difference between a class rule and a town rule, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Name a real statute, regulation and bylaw and how each is different, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Trace a real rule to whether it comes from a statute, regulation or bylaw, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else where a real rule they follow actually comes from.

themes.description: Who sues whom, who prosecutes, and why the same act can be both — the two systems' different players, standards and stakes.
themes.transfer_check: Sort five real scenarios into civil, criminal or both, naming the parties and the standard of proof for each.

bands.K–2: Say the difference between an accident and breaking a rule on purpose, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Explain why some wrongs are 'against a person' and some are 'against everyone', with an adult.
bands.6–8: Sort three real cases into civil and criminal correctly, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain, for a real news story, whether it is a civil or criminal matter and why.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why the same real act could be both a civil and a criminal matter.

themes.description: What courtrooms actually do all day — the hierarchy, who the people in it are, and what an ordinary hearing looks like.
themes.transfer_check: Observe a real public hearing (in person or official stream) and report who did what, in the correct terms.

bands.K–2: Draw a picture of a courtroom with an adult, naming one person in it.
bands.3–5: Name two people who work in a real courtroom, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Explain what a real court actually does day to day, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain the real hierarchy of courts and who hears what, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else what happens inside a real courtroom on an ordinary day.

themes.description: Legal research for civilians: official sources, current versions, and the difference between the law and a blog about the law.
themes.transfer_check: Answer one real legal question about your own life from primary official sources, citing the provision itself.

bands.K–2: Look up a simple rule in a book with an adult's help.
bands.3–5: Find a real rule using an official website, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Find a real current rule from an official source and confirm it's current, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Do real legal research as a civilian, on your own, from official sources.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to find and confirm a real current rule for themselves.

themes.description: Limitation periods, notice windows and appeal clocks — why being right runs out, and diarising the dates that matter.
themes.transfer_check: For three real claim types, find the applicable time limit where you live and compute the deadline from a given event date.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult why some tickets or forms have a due date.
bands.3–5: Name one deadline that matters to your family, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Identify a real limitation period or notice window on a real matter, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Track a real deadline — limitation, notice, appeal — on your own, without missing it.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why a real right can expire if you miss its deadline.

themes.description: Legal aid, law centres, pro bono, ombudsmen and fixed-fee clinics — the map of low-cost help and who qualifies.
themes.transfer_check: Map the free and low-cost legal help available for one problem type at your own address, with eligibility rules verified.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult who helps people who can't pay a lawyer.
bands.3–5: Name one place that offers free legal help, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Find a real legal aid or pro bono service for a real need, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Find and use a real affordable legal help option on your own.
bands.11–12: Guide someone else to a real free or fixed-fee legal help service.

themes.description: Setting out a grievance formally: facts, ask, deadline — the letter that resolves most disputes before any court sees them.
themes.transfer_check: Draft a complete letter before action for a real or realistic dispute, meeting the format a court would later respect.

bands.K–2: Help write a short, polite complaint letter with an adult.
bands.3–5: Write a simple complaint with a fact and an ask, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Write a real letter before action with facts, ask and deadline, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write a real formal grievance letter on your own that gets a response.
bands.11–12: Help someone else write a real letter before action that states a clear ask and deadline.

themes.theme: Small claims: court without the lawyers
themes.description: The small-claims track end to end — filing, fees, evidence bundles and the hearing where you speak for yourself.
themes.transfer_check: Prepare a complete mock small claim: forms filled, evidence bundled, and your three-minute case stated aloud.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what happens when two neighbours can't agree and go to a small court.
bands.3–5: Explain what small claims court is for, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Walk through a real small-claims filing step, with a checker.
bands.9–10: File or prepare a real small-claims case on your own, from evidence to filing.
bands.11–12: Guide someone else through a real small-claims case end to end.

themes.theme: Mediation and the deal that beats the verdict
themes.description: Negotiated and mediated settlement — why most disputes should end in a room, not a courtroom, and how to settle well.
themes.transfer_check: Take one side of a role-played dispute through a structured mediation to a written settlement both sides sign.

bands.K–2: Help two friends work out a disagreement without a grown-up deciding for them.
bands.3–5: Explain why talking it out can beat a strict ruling, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Explain why a real dispute might be better settled than tried, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Prepare for a real mediated settlement on your own, weighing it against a trial.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why most real disputes should settle rather than go to trial.

themes.theme: When the law itself is the problem
themes.description: Challenging rules: consultation responses, judicial review in outline, and the civic route from unjust rule to changed rule.
themes.transfer_check: Find one live consultation or proposed rule affecting you and submit (or fully draft) a reasoned formal response.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult about a rule you think is unfair.
bands.3–5: Write down why a rule seems unfair, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Write a real consultation response to a rule you think is wrong, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Challenge a real rule on your own — consultation, review or otherwise.
bands.11–12: Help someone else challenge a real rule they believe is the problem.

themes.description: Offer, acceptance, consideration, intention — the ingredients that turn words into obligations, including the ones spoken aloud.
themes.transfer_check: Analyse five everyday exchanges and rule which formed a contract, naming the missing ingredient where none did.

bands.K–2: Shake hands on a trade of toys with a friend, with an adult watching.
bands.3–5: Explain what makes a trade fair and agreed, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Name the ingredients of a real binding agreement, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain, for a real deal, whether offer, acceptance and consideration are all present.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else the ingredients that make a real promise legally binding.

themes.description: A method for real documents: parties, obligations, money, term, exit, liability — the six answers to extract from any contract.
themes.transfer_check: Extract the six-answer summary from a real contract you are actually subject to, in one page a friend could rely on.

bands.K–2: Look at a simple form with an adult before anyone signs it.
bands.3–5: Find the names of the people in a real simple agreement, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Find the parties, obligations and money in a real document, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read a real document methodically for parties, obligations, money and term, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else a method for reading a real document before they sign.

themes.description: Auto-renewal, unilateral change, arbitration, indemnity, liquidated damages — the standard traps and the flags they fly.
themes.transfer_check: Locate and explain three bite-clauses across real contracts or terms of service, and state what each costs you if triggered.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what a 'gotcha' rule in a game's fine print might mean.
bands.3–5: Spot one surprising rule buried in fine print, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Identify a real auto-renewal or arbitration clause in a document, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify and evaluate a real biting clause — renewal, arbitration, indemnity — on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else what a real biting clause could cost them.

themes.theme: Terms of service: the contract nobody reads
themes.description: What you actually agree to online — licences to your content, data terms, termination at will — and the summaries that surface it.
themes.transfer_check: Audit the terms of one service you use daily and report the three most consequential things you had agreed to unknowingly.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what happens when you tap 'I agree' on an app.
bands.3–5: Find one real thing an app's terms let it do, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Find what a real app's terms actually grant it over your content, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read a real terms of service and identify what you actually agreed to, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else what a real 'I agree' click actually commits them to.

themes.description: What is negotiable (more than you think), asking in writing, and the walk-away number decided in advance.
themes.transfer_check: Negotiate one real agreement's term (price, date, clause) with the exchange documented, or run the full role-play to signed changes.

bands.K–2: Ask a friend if a trade could be a little different before agreeing, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Ask for a small change to a deal before agreeing, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Propose a real change to a real agreement in writing, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Negotiate a real term of a real agreement in writing, on your own.
bands.11–12: Coach someone else on negotiating a real term before they sign.

themes.theme: Breach: when the other side fails
themes.description: Material versus minor breach, mitigation, and the remedies ladder from cure period to damages.
themes.transfer_check: For a real or case-study breach, classify it, state your mitigation duty, and draft the remedy demand in the right order.

bands.K–2: Say what happens when a friend breaks a promise in a game, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Explain the difference between a small broken promise and a big one, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Sort a real broken promise into major or minor breach, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify a real breach and the remedy it opens up, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real remedies available when the other side fails.

themes.description: Cancellation rights, cooling-off periods, termination clauses and the exit executed cleanly versus the exit that costs you.
themes.transfer_check: Exit or mock-exit one real subscription or agreement using its own terms, on time, in writing, with proof retained.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult how to return something you no longer want.
bands.3–5: Find the return policy on a real receipt, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Find a real cancellation right or cooling-off period, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Exercise a real cancellation right or termination clause on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how a real cooling-off period actually works.

themes.theme: Deposits, guarantees and standing behind others
themes.description: Security deposits, guarantors and co-signing — the promises that activate when someone else fails.
themes.transfer_check: Explain a real guarantee or deposit's exact trigger and exposure, and advise a role-played friend asked to co-sign, with reasons.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what a deposit is when renting a bike.
bands.3–5: Explain why a deposit is held and when it comes back, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain a real guarantor's or co-signer's obligation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Evaluate a real deposit, guarantee or co-sign request before agreeing to it.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real risk of standing behind another person's promise.

themes.theme: The informal deal with family and friends
themes.description: Loans to brothers, flats shared with friends — why the closest deals need the clearest writing, and the note that saves the relationship.
themes.transfer_check: Draft a fair one-page written agreement for a real or realistic informal arrangement between people who trust each other.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult why it's good to write down a loan between friends.
bands.3–5: Write down a simple loan agreement with a friend, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Write a real simple agreement for a loan or shared flat, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Put a real informal deal with family or friends into writing, on your own.
bands.11–12: Help someone else formalise a real informal deal to avoid a later dispute.

themes.theme: Signing for the future: powers and wills
themes.description: Powers of attorney, advance decisions and wills — the documents that speak when you cannot, and what happens without them.
themes.transfer_check: Complete the will-and-powers checklist for a named adult: what exists, what is missing, and the exact route to fix one gap.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what a will is, in simple words.
bands.3–5: Explain why grown-ups plan for who decides things later, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain what a real power of attorney or advance decision does, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain the real documents — power of attorney, advance decision, will — and their purpose.
bands.11–12: Guide someone else through why and how these real future-signing documents matter.

tracks.name: The consumer: buying, returning, being made whole

themes.theme: What you are owed when you buy
themes.description: Satisfactory quality, as described, fit for purpose — the rights attached to every purchase whether the shop likes it or not.
themes.transfer_check: For three real purchases, state the statutory rights attached to each and the remedy ladder if it fails.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what a fair toy purchase should include.
bands.3–5: Name what a real product should be — working and as described, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain a real product's right to be of satisfactory quality, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Assert a real right — quality, as described, fit for purpose — on your own purchase.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real rights that come with any purchase.

themes.description: The store's goodwill policy and your legal rights are different things — knowing which you are invoking and when each is stronger.
themes.transfer_check: Handle one real or staged return correctly, explicitly identifying whether you used policy or law, and why.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult if a store has to take something back.
bands.3–5: Explain the difference between a store's kindness and a real rule, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Distinguish a real store's return policy from your actual legal right, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Assert your real legal right when a store's policy falls short, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real difference between store goodwill and legal right.

themes.description: Repair, replace, refund — the sequence, the burden of proof windows, and the evidence to gather before the second failure.
themes.transfer_check: Run a real or mock faulty-goods claim through the full sequence in writing, with the evidence file that wins it.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what to do with a broken toy from a store.
bands.3–5: Explain the order of repair, replace, refund, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Follow the real repair-replace-refund sequence for a faulty item, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Handle a real faulty purchase on your own, in the right order, with proof.
bands.11–12: Guide someone else through a real faulty-goods claim, sequence and proof.

themes.description: Reasonable care and skill — holding builders, salons, garages and installers to the standard, and pricing the put-right.
themes.transfer_check: Draft the complaint and remedy demand for a real or case-study substandard service, quantifying the cost to cure.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what to do if a haircut goes badly.
bands.3–5: Explain that a service should be done with reasonable care, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain a real service provider's duty of reasonable care and skill, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Hold a real service provider to reasonable care and skill, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how to hold a real tradesperson accountable for poor work.

themes.description: Online, phone and doorstep purchases — the cooling-off rights, the return-shipping rules and the exceptions that surprise.
themes.transfer_check: Exercise (or fully mock) a cooling-off cancellation for an online purchase inside its window, with the notices done right.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult why buying online is different from a shop.
bands.3–5: Explain what a cooling-off period is for online buying, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain a real cooling-off right for a real online or doorstep purchase, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Exercise a real cooling-off right on a real distance purchase, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how real distance-selling rights protect a buyer.

themes.description: Card protections, chargeback windows and why how you pay changes what you can recover when it goes wrong.
themes.transfer_check: File or fully draft one chargeback or card-protection claim with the transaction evidence assembled to standard.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult why paying with a card can be safer than cash.
bands.3–5: Explain one protection a card offers that cash doesn't, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain a real chargeback window and card protection, with a checker.
bands.9–10: File a real chargeback or use card protection on your own, within the window.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why how you pay changes your real protection.

themes.description: Escalation done properly: the right person, the factual timeline, the specific ask and the deadline — firm without fury.
themes.transfer_check: Write and send (or finalise) a real complaint with timeline, evidence, ask and deadline, and log the response against it.

bands.K–2: Practice a polite complaint about a broken toy, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Write a simple, factual complaint, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Write a real complaint that escalates properly with facts and timeline, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Escalate a real complaint to the right person on your own, and get a result.
bands.11–12: Coach someone else on writing a real complaint that actually gets a result.

themes.theme: The ombudsman and the free referee
themes.description: Sector ombudsmen and ADR schemes — the free escalation most consumers never use, and how to hand them a winnable file.
themes.transfer_check: Identify the correct ombudsman for one real dispute type and prepare the complete referral file to its requirements.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult who helps when a company won't fix things.
bands.3–5: Name a free helper who settles disputes, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Find a real sector ombudsman or ADR scheme for a real dispute, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Escalate a real unresolved dispute to a real ombudsman on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how a real ombudsman scheme works and when to use it.

themes.description: Fake shops, counterfeit goods, subscription traps and recovery scams — the purchase that was never a purchase.
themes.transfer_check: Autopsy one real scam listing or trap: mark its tells, state the reporting channels used, and the victim's actual recovery options.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult before buying anything from someone online.
bands.3–5: Name one sign of a fake online shop, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Identify a real fake shop or counterfeit listing, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Recognise and avoid a real scam seller on your own before paying.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real warning signs of a scam seller.

themes.theme: Debt collection and your actual obligations
themes.description: What collectors may and may not do, statute-barred debt, and the difference between owing and being harassed.
themes.transfer_check: Respond to a real or scripted collection letter correctly: verify the debt, know the rules the collector must follow, and draft the reply.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what happens if a bill isn't paid.
bands.3–5: Explain that debt collectors must follow rules too, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain a real collector's limits and a real statute-barred debt, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Verify a real debt collection claim against your actual obligations, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else what a real debt collector may and may not do.

tracks.name: Work: the deal behind the job

themes.description: The status categories, the rights attached to each, and the misclassification that quietly removes protections.
themes.transfer_check: Classify three real working arrangements (yours or case studies) by status and list two rights that change across them.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what different jobs a grown-up can have at work.
bands.3–5: Name a difference between a full-time job and doing odd jobs, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Sort a real job into employee, worker or contractor, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify a real job's status and the rights that attach to it, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real rights that come with each work status.

themes.description: Pay, hours, notice, probation, restrictive covenants — reading the job offer as the contract it is.
themes.transfer_check: Produce the six-answer summary of a real employment contract or offer, flagging any clause you would question before signing.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what a work agreement says about pay.
bands.3–5: Find the pay and hours in a real simple job description, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Find pay, hours, notice and probation in a real contract, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read a real employment contract for pay, hours, notice and restrictions, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to read a real employment contract before signing.

themes.description: Minimum wage arithmetic, payslip reading, unlawful deductions and the overtime that never appears.
themes.transfer_check: Audit a real payslip against contract and law — rate, hours, deductions — and draft the query for any discrepancy found.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult how you'd know if you got paid the right amount.
bands.3–5: Check a simple pay calculation against a rate, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Check a real payslip against minimum wage arithmetic, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Verify a real payslip on your own and flag an unlawful deduction.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how to check a real payslip for errors or unlawful deductions.

themes.description: Working time limits, rest rights and the pressure to be always available — the boundaries the law already drew.
themes.transfer_check: Compare one real working pattern to the applicable limits and rest rights, and script the conversation any breach requires.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult why workers get breaks during a long day.
bands.3–5: Explain why rest matters during a work day, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Explain a real working-time limit and rest right, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Assert a real rest right on your own when pressured to skip it.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real limits on hours and the right to rest.

themes.theme: Leave: the time that is yours
themes.description: Holiday, sickness, parental and carer leave — what accrues, what needs notice and what cannot be refused.
themes.transfer_check: Compute a real worker's leave entitlement for the year and correctly process (or mock) one request and one sickness absence.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what happens when someone is sick and can't go to work.
bands.3–5: Name one kind of leave a worker can take, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Explain a real type of leave — holiday, sick, parental — and what it accrues, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Calculate your own real leave entitlement and what it accrues.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how real leave entitlements work and accrue.

themes.description: The protected characteristics, direct and indirect discrimination, and reasonable adjustment as a right rather than a favour.
themes.transfer_check: Analyse two case-study workplace scenarios: identify the protected ground, the discrimination type, and the remedy route for each.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult why it's wrong to treat someone unfairly for who they are.
bands.3–5: Name one protected characteristic, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Identify a real example of direct or indirect discrimination, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Recognise a real discrimination case and the protected ground involved, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real protected characteristics and what discrimination looks like.

themes.description: Naming it, logging it, reporting it — the evidence diary and the routes inside and beyond the employer.
themes.transfer_check: Build a correct incident log from a scripted harassment scenario and map its escalation route through and past the employer.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult if someone at school keeps being mean to you.
bands.3–5: Explain why you should write down what happened if someone is unkind, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Log a real incident with facts and dates, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Report a real workplace harassment incident on your own, with a proper evidence log.
bands.11–12: Guide someone else through reporting real workplace harassment properly.

themes.description: Investigations, hearings, accompaniment and appeals — what a fair procedure owes you when the employer moves against you.
themes.transfer_check: Role-play the employee side of a disciplinary hearing with a companion, exercising each procedural right at the correct moment.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what happens when a rule is broken at school, step by step.
bands.3–5: Name one step of a fair process when someone breaks a rule, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain a real fair disciplinary process — investigation, hearing, appeal, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Navigate a real disciplinary process on your own, knowing your rights at each step.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else what a real fair disciplinary process must include.

themes.description: Notice, redundancy rules, unfair dismissal and the settlement agreement — the endings, and the rights attached to each.
themes.transfer_check: For one real or case-study dismissal, determine its type, the entitlements owed, and the challenge deadline, with the first letter drafted.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what happens if a grown-up's job ends.
bands.3–5: Explain what notice means when a job ends, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Explain real redundancy rules and unfair dismissal, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Evaluate a real job loss for notice, redundancy or unfair dismissal, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real options when a job ends unfairly.

themes.description: Unions, collective bargaining and protected activity — what workers may lawfully do together and how that changes the deal.
themes.transfer_check: Find the recognised union or body for one real workplace and explain what protected steps starting to organise there would involve.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult why workers sometimes join a group together.
bands.3–5: Explain what a union is for, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Explain a real protected organising activity, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain, for a real workplace, what collective bargaining actually changes.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real rights workers have when they organise together.

themes.description: The charter, constitution or convention where you live — the actual named rights, and what each does and does not protect.
themes.transfer_check: For your own jurisdiction, list the instrument and five named rights, matching each to one real situation it governs.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult to name one right you have.
bands.3–5: Name two rights you have, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Find where your real rights are written down, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify, for a real situation, which of your written rights applies.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else where their real rights come from and what they say.

themes.description: Stop, search and questioning — what officers may require, what you must provide, and the calm scripts that protect everyone.
themes.transfer_check: Role-play two police encounters correctly: state your actual obligations, exercise your actual rights, and note the record to make after.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what to do if a police officer talks to you.
bands.3–5: Name one thing you can calmly say if stopped, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Explain what a real officer may and may not require during a stop, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain your real rights during a stop and search, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else exactly what happens, and what rights apply, during a real stop.

themes.theme: Arrest and the hours that follow
themes.description: The caution, the phone call, the duty lawyer and the custody clock — the rights that exist precisely when you are least able to look them up.
themes.transfer_check: Recite and apply the post-arrest rights sequence for your jurisdiction in a staged scenario, including invoking the duty lawyer.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult who you'd call if something scary happened.
bands.3–5: Name the one phone call you'd want if something went wrong, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain a real caution and the right to a phone call, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain the real sequence — caution, call, duty lawyer, custody — on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else what actually happens in the real hours after an arrest.

themes.description: Assembly and speech rights, notification rules, police powers at protests and the line where protection ends.
themes.transfer_check: Plan a lawful demonstration for a cause: the notifications, the rules on route and sound, and the legal-observer arrangements.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult why people sometimes gather to share an opinion outside.
bands.3–5: Explain what a peaceful protest is for, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Explain a real notification rule for a public gathering, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain real assembly and speech rights and their limits, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real rules and rights around a public protest.

themes.theme: Your file: what the state holds
themes.description: Records access rights — police records, agency files, credit and health data — and the request that opens them.
themes.transfer_check: Submit (or fully prepare) one real access request to a public body for your own records, to its formal requirements.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult if the school keeps notes about you.
bands.3–5: Name one record an agency might keep about a person, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Find what a real agency holds on you and how to request it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Request a real record the state or an agency holds about you, on your own.
bands.11–12: Guide someone else through requesting their real state or agency file.

themes.description: Benefits refused, permits denied, fines issued — reading the decision letter, the reasons, and the review and appeal ladder.
themes.transfer_check: Take one real or case-study adverse decision and draft the first-stage challenge inside its deadline, addressing the stated reasons.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what to do if a rule seems to be applied unfairly to you.
bands.3–5: Explain one way to ask a decision to be looked at again, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Read a real official decision letter for the appeal route, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Appeal a real official decision on your own, using the stated route.
bands.11–12: Guide someone else through appealing a real official decision.

themes.theme: Voting and the machinery of elections
themes.description: Registration, eligibility, the ballot's journey and the count — the process behind the cross in the box.
themes.transfer_check: Verify your own registration, explain your ballot's path from booth to count, and correctly handle one edge case (moving, absence, spoiled paper).

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what happens when grown-ups vote.
bands.3–5: Explain why a ballot is counted carefully, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Explain real voter registration and eligibility rules, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain a real ballot's journey from casting to counting, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real machinery that makes an election count.

themes.theme: Jury service and the citizen's bench
themes.description: Selection, duties, deliberation and the juror's oath — the one week the justice system runs on you.
themes.transfer_check: From a case summary, deliberate in a mock jury to a verdict, applying the standard of proof and the judge's directions.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what a jury does in a courtroom.
bands.3–5: Explain why regular people help decide a real case, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain a real juror's selection and duties, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain the real deliberation process and a juror's oath, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why jury service matters and what it actually involves.

themes.description: Citizenship, residence and visas in outline — what status determines, and helping someone find competent immigration help.
themes.transfer_check: For one case-study person, identify what their status allows and bars, and locate the regulated adviser route for their question.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what it means to be a citizen of a place.
bands.3–5: Name one difference between a visitor and a citizen, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain a real status — citizenship, residence, visa — in outline, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain what a real immigration status determines, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real outline of citizenship, residence and visa status.

themes.description: Freedom of information, public meetings, complaints against officials and the press — the accountability toolkit in civilian hands.
themes.transfer_check: File (or fully draft) one real freedom-of-information request on a matter you care about, scoped so it cannot be refused as too broad.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult how people find out what a government is doing.
bands.3–5: Name one way people can ask a government a question, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Use a real freedom-of-information request or public meeting, with a checker.
bands.9–10: File a real freedom-of-information request or complaint against power, on your own.
bands.11–12: Guide someone else through holding real power to account with a real tool.
